rw: Higher flour prices raise the bakers' input costs, so they supply less bread at every price, which shifts the supply curve to the left.

ww.A new, faster oven: A faster oven raises productivity and lowers the cost per loaf, so bakers supply more bread at each price and the curve shifts right.
ww.More bakeries opening up: More bakeries means more sellers in the market, so the quantity supplied at every price grows and the supply curve shifts right, not left.
ww.A tax cut for bakers: A tax cut lowers bakers' costs and raises their after-tax return, so they supply more bread at every price and the curve shifts right.

rw: A surplus exists when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded at a given price, leaving unsold goods that push the price down toward equilibrium.

ww.Quantity demanded exceeds quantity suppl: This describes a shortage, not a surplus, because buyers want more units than sellers offer at that price, which pushes the price up instead.
ww.Supply equals demand in the market at a: Supply equal to demand is market equilibrium, where there is no gap and no pressure on price, so nothing is left over unsold.
ww.A government budget gain over the whole: A government budget gain is a fiscal surplus, which compares tax revenue with spending over a year, and it is not about quantities in one market.

rw: A shortage occurs when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price, so some buyers go unserved and the price tends to rise.

ww.A lack of workers in a state or region o: A lack of workers is a labor shortage in one region, which is a narrower idea than the market shortage defined by quantities at a price.
ww.Quantity supplied exceeds quantity deman: This is a surplus, since sellers offer more than buyers want at that price, leaving unsold goods, while a shortage has demand above supply.
ww.Supply equals demand in the market at th: Supply equal to demand is equilibrium, where the market clears with no unmet demand and no unsold goods, so no shortage exists at that price.

rw: At a price below equilibrium buyers want more than sellers offer, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a shortage develops.

ww.A surplus develops: A surplus appears when price is above equilibrium, because sellers offer more than buyers want, while a price below equilibrium draws extra buyers instead.
ww.Equilibrium holds: Equilibrium holds only at the price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, and a price set below it breaks that balance, so it cannot hold.
ww.Supply rises at once: A lower price gives sellers less reason to produce, so quantity supplied falls along the supply curve, and it does not rise at once.

rw: A binding ceiling below equilibrium holds the price down, so buyers want more than sellers supply, and quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, which is a shortage.

ww.Lower demand: A ceiling below equilibrium makes the good cheaper, which raises the quantity demanded along the demand curve, so demand does not fall and the effect is reversed.
ww.A surplus: A surplus needs a price above equilibrium, such as a binding price floor, while a ceiling below equilibrium creates the opposite gap of excess demand.
ww.Higher quality: Sellers earn less at the capped price and may cut costs, so quality tends to fall rather than rise, and the shortage often brings lines and rationing.

rw: Price elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price, usually computed as the percent change in quantity over the percent change in price.

ww.The share of income that is taxed by the: That describes a tax rate on income, which is a fiscal measure, and it says nothing about how buyers react when the price of a good changes.
ww.The cost of making one more unit of a pr: That describes marginal cost, the added expense of making one more unit, which is a producer cost concept and not the buyer response measured by elasticity.
ww.How quickly prices rise each year across: That describes the inflation rate, a rise in the general price level over time, while elasticity concerns the reaction of buyers to a change in one price.

rw: With elastic demand the percent fall in quantity demanded is larger than the percent rise in price, so price times quantity shrinks and total revenue falls.

ww.Rise: Revenue rises only when demand is inelastic, since buyers barely cut purchases, but with elastic demand the quantity drop outweighs the higher price, so it does not rise.
ww.Hold: Revenue holds steady only when demand is unit elastic, where the percent drop in quantity equals the percent rise in price, and elastic demand is more responsive than that.
ww.Double: Doubling is not possible, because a price rise with elastic demand cuts the quantity sold by a larger percent, so revenue shrinks and never doubles.

rw: Insulin is a medical necessity with no real substitute, so diabetics keep buying it even when the price jumps, which makes demand inelastic.

ww.Designer sunglasses: Designer sunglasses are a luxury with many close substitutes, and buyers can easily delay or skip them when prices rise, so demand is elastic.
ww.A particular snack chip: A particular snack chip has many rival snacks, so shoppers switch easily when its price rises, which makes the demand for it elastic.
ww.A specific brand of candy: A specific brand of candy competes with many other brands and sweets, so buyers can switch readily, and the demand for it is elastic.

rw: When many close substitutes exist, buyers easily switch away after a price rise, so quantity demanded drops sharply, and that makes demand more elastic.

ww.Makes demand disappear: Substitutes do not erase demand, since buyers still want the product category, but they switch to other options when the price rises, so demand does not vanish.
ww.Has no effect on demand: Substitutes strongly affect elasticity, because buyers can leave for alternatives, so claiming no effect ignores the main reason demand responds to price changes.
ww.Makes demand more inelastic: Inelastic demand needs few substitutes, like medicine, so many close substitutes push elasticity the other way and make demand more elastic, not more inelastic.

rw: High setup costs make one firm serving the whole market cheaper than several, which is the definition of a natural monopoly, as with local water.

ww.An oligopoly firm: An oligopoly has a few competing firms, but this town has just one water utility, so the market has a single seller and not a few.
ww.Pure competition: Pure competition has many sellers of identical goods, but a town with a single water utility has no rivals, so it is not purely competitive.
ww.Perfect competition: Perfect competition needs many sellers and easy entry, while one water utility with huge setup costs blocks entry and serves the whole town alone.

rw: A few large commercial airlines dominate air travel, with high entry barriers and strategic pricing against each other, which are the marks of an oligopoly.

ww.Local farmers markets: Farmers markets have many small sellers with easy entry, so no single seller holds much power, which looks like competition and not an oligopoly of a few big firms.
ww.Wheat farming in a state: Wheat farming has thousands of producers selling identical grain at the market price, which matches perfect competition and not a market ruled by a few firms.
ww.Local lawn care services: Lawn care has many small local providers and low barriers to start, so there are far too many sellers to count as an oligopoly.

rw: Collusion is a secret agreement among firms to fix prices or limit output, which acts like a monopoly, and it is typically illegal under antitrust law.

ww.Firms merging legally with each other in: A merger is a legal combination of firms, usually reviewed by regulators, and it is an open ownership change, not the secret price agreement called collusion.
ww.Firms exporting goods to buyers in other: Exporting goods to buyers abroad is ordinary international trade, and it involves no agreement among rival firms to set prices or restrict output.
ww.Firms competing on price openly so buyer: Firms openly competing on price is healthy rivalry that lowers prices for buyers, which is the opposite of collusion, where rivals secretly agree to avoid such competition.

rw: Total cost is fixed cost plus variable cost, so $2,000 rent plus $0.50 times 1,000 loaves, which is $500, gives $2,500.

ww.$2,000: The $2,000 is only the fixed rent and leaves out the variable flour cost of $0.50 times 1,000 loaves, which is $500, so total cost is higher.
ww.$500: The $500 is only the flour cost (1,000 loaves times $0.50) and ignores the $2,000 rent, which must be paid no matter how many loaves are baked.
ww.$3,000: The $3,000 would need $1,000 in flour costs, but 1,000 loaves at $0.50 each cost only $500, so $2,000 plus $500 is $2,500, not $3,000.

rw: A profit-maximizing firm produces up to where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, since each unit before that adds more revenue than cost and later units add less.

ww.Where price is highest so units earn the: The highest price does not maximize profit, because higher prices cut sales, and profit depends on revenue minus cost across all units, not on the top price.
ww.Where fixed cost ends for the whole firm: Where fixed cost ends is not a decision rule, since fixed costs do not change with output, so they do not tell a firm how much to produce.
ww.Where sales are zero for the whole firm: Producing nothing earns no revenue and leaves the firm to pay its fixed costs, so zero sales cannot maximize profit except in unusual shutdown cases.

rw: Economies of scale mean average cost per unit falls as output rises, because fixed costs are spread over more units and larger production brings efficiencies.

ww.Costs that never change in any year: Costs that never change describe fixed costs, which are only part of total cost and say nothing about how average cost changes as output grows.
ww.Costs of weighing goods for sale: This is a play on the word scale, since economies of scale have nothing to do with weighing goods, and refer to cost savings from producing more.
ww.Higher average costs as output grows: Higher average costs as output grows describe diseconomies of scale, the opposite situation, where a firm becomes too large and costs per unit rise.

rw: Diminishing returns means each added worker adds less output than the one before when other inputs stay fixed, which matches cooks crowding a small kitchen.

ww.Inflation spiral: An inflation spiral is a general rise in prices feeding wage demands, which is a macroeconomic effect and not about the output of added cooks in a kitchen.
ww.Economies of scale: Economies of scale mean average cost falls as output grows, but here added cooks produce less extra food each, which points to rising marginal cost.
ww.Perfect competition: Perfect competition is a market structure with many sellers, and it does not describe the falling extra output from adding workers to a fixed kitchen.

rw: Money serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account for pricing goods, and a store of value that holds purchasing power over time.

ww.Only a tool for taxes and fees paid by t: Taxes and fees are a use of government finance, but money's functions are broader, so saying it is only a tool for taxes leaves out its main roles.
ww.Only a way to decorate a wallet, with li: Decoration is not an economic function, and money's real value comes from its use in trade and saving, so this option ignores its actual roles.
ww.Only a measure of weight for goods, gold: Money is not a measure of physical weight, and goods and coins are priced in units of account, so this confuses weights with value.

rw: The money supply is the total amount of money in an economy at a given time, including currency and deposits that people can use to spend.

ww.The price of gold only, per ounce sold: The price of gold is a commodity price and not the quantity of money circulating, so it is not the money supply and is not defined per ounce.
ww.The number of banks in a state or countr: The number of banks counts institutions, not the amount of money in circulation, so it says nothing about how much money people hold and spend.
ww.The wages of workers in the economy: Wages are a price of labor, and the money supply measures the quantity of money in the economy, not what workers are paid for their time.

rw: The Fed pays banks with new reserves, and banks can lend them out, which expands deposits through lending, so the money supply increases.

ww.No change: When the Fed buys bonds it pays banks with newly created reserves, which adds money to the banking system, so the money supply does change.
ww.It is destroyed: Money is not destroyed in a bond purchase, since the Fed pays banks with newly created reserves, and money is destroyed when the Fed sells bonds instead.
ww.It decreases: A decrease would come from the Fed selling bonds, which takes reserves out of banks, while buying bonds does the reverse by putting reserves in.

rw: The reserve requirement is the fraction of customer deposits a bank must hold in reserve and cannot lend out, which limits how much it can create through lending.

ww.The fee for ATM use at a bank branch eac: An ATM fee is a service charge a bank sets for customers using a machine, and it has nothing to do with the reserves the Fed requires.
ww.The tax paid on deposits to the state ea: A tax on deposits would be paid to the state, but the reserve requirement is a rule on liquid funds banks keep, and not a payment to anyone.
ww.The interest paid to savers, set by the: Interest paid to savers is set by banks through competition, and it is separate from the reserve requirement, which the central bank sets for safety.

rw: A higher federal funds rate pushes up the rates banks charge, so loans cost more, and households and firms borrow and spend less, slowing demand.

ww.Borrowing becomes cheaper and spending r: Cheaper borrowing comes from a lower federal funds rate, so a rate increase has the opposite effect by making loans more expensive and cooling spending.
ww.Savings earn nothing at all for the acco: A higher rate usually lifts the interest paid on savings, not drops it to zero, so savers tend to earn more and not nothing.
ww.Prices rise faster in the whole economy: Raising rates is used to fight inflation, since it reduces spending and cools price growth, so it does not make prices rise faster for years.

rw: GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given year, which measures the size of output.

ww.The government's yearly spending only, w: Government spending is only one component of GDP, along with consumption, investment and net exports, so it cannot stand for total output by itself.
ww.The value of stock markets around the wo: Stock market value measures the worth of listed companies, which is a financial measure, while GDP counts output of goods and services produced in a country.
ww.The total number of workers employed in: The number of workers employed is a labor market measure, and GDP is measured in money value of output, so headcount alone does not define it.

rw: A new car produced and sold this year is a final good made in the current year, so its value is counted in GDP.

ww.Stocks bought on an exchange today: Buying stocks transfers ownership of existing assets and does not produce new goods or services, so it is a financial transaction and not part of GDP.
ww.Money gifted between friends or kin: A gift between friends is a transfer payment with no good or service produced in exchange, so it adds nothing to current output or GDP.
ww.A used car resold this year by a dealer: A used car was produced in an earlier year, so its resale is not new production and is excluded, though the dealer's service fee may count.

rw: Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, so it compares output across years using constant prices, which shows true growth in goods and services.

ww.GDP measured only in cash: Measuring GDP only in cash is not a concept in economics, and real GDP is defined by adjusting for inflation, not by the form of payment.
ww.GDP of just one city or region: GDP of a single city or region is regional GDP, which is a scope question, while real GDP concerns removing inflation from the output measure.
ww.GDP before any adjustment: GDP before any adjustment for price changes is nominal GDP, measured at current prices, so it is the opposite of real GDP.

rw: A recession is a significant decline in economic activity across the economy, shown in output, jobs and incomes, lasting several months or longer.

ww.A single bad sales day for one store in: One bad sales day at one store is a local, short event, and a recession involves a broad decline across the whole economy lasting months.
ww.A brief rise in stock prices that lasts: A brief rise in stock prices is not a recession, which is a decline in economic activity rather than a short gain in one financial market.
ww.A period of rapid growth in output, jobs: Rapid growth in output, jobs and incomes describes an economic boom or expansion, which is the opposite of a recession.

rw: In a recession demand falls, firms cut production and lay off workers, so unemployment rises, which is a typical sign of the downturn.

ww.Rapid wage growth: Rapid wage growth belongs to booms with tight labor markets, while recessions bring weak demand for workers, so pay growth tends to slow or stall.
ww.Falling joblessness: Falling joblessness happens during expansions, when firms hire more, whereas recessions cause layoffs and rising unemployment, so this describes the opposite.
ww.Rising consumer demand: Rising consumer demand marks an expansion, while in a recession households cut spending because of lower incomes and uncertainty, so demand usually falls.

rw: The unemployment rate is the number of jobless people actively looking for work divided by the labor force, shown as a percent.

ww.The percent of all people without jobs,: The rate is not measured against everyone, because children and retirees are outside the labor force, so counting them would understate unemployment.
ww.The percent of workers who quit their jo: Workers who quit are not necessarily unemployed, since many move to other jobs, so quits are not the measure of joblessness in the labor force.
ww.The percent of all wages that are taxed: Taxes on wages concern the tax system and have no connection to counting who has a job, so this cannot define the unemployment rate.

rw: Structural unemployment comes from a mismatch between workers' skills or locations and the jobs available, and it can last long without retraining.

ww.Joblessness during recessions and other: Joblessness in recessions is cyclical unemployment, which rises and falls with the business cycle and not from a skills mismatch in the labor market.
ww.Joblessness while moving between jobs, s: Short joblessness while moving between jobs is frictional unemployment, which ends when a new job is found and is not caused by missing skills.
ww.Joblessness from seasonal work in farmin: Joblessness from seasonal work patterns is seasonal unemployment, which follows the calendar, and it differs from a lasting mismatch of skills and jobs.

rw: Robots replacing workers who lack the new skills is a mismatch between skills and available jobs, which defines structural unemployment.

ww.Frictional unemployment: Frictional unemployment is the short search time between jobs, while workers whose skills no longer fit new jobs face a lasting problem, which is not friction.
ww.Cyclical unemployment: Cyclical unemployment comes from weak demand in a recession, but here the factory closed because technology changed the skills needed, not because demand fell.
ww.Seasonal unemployment: Seasonal unemployment follows regular yearly patterns, like farm or tourism work, and a factory replacing workers with robots has no seasonal cause.

rw: Pay grows 2% but prices grow 5%, so real purchasing power changes by about minus 3%, and the worker can afford less than before.

ww.It doubles: Purchasing power cannot double when prices rise faster than pay, since the real wage depends on pay compared with prices, which shows a loss.
ww.No change: Purchasing power would stay the same only if pay rose as fast as prices, and 2% pay growth lags 5% inflation, so there is a change.
ww.It rises: Pay rising 2% while prices rise 5% leaves workers able to buy less, so purchasing power cannot rise.

rw: The consumer price index measures the average change over time in prices paid by consumers for a basket of goods and services, and it is used to gauge inflation.

ww.A rating of products by quality for buye: A rating of products by quality is a consumer review, not a price measure, and the consumer price index tracks changes in the prices of goods.
ww.A list of stock prices on the exchange e: A list of stock prices is a stock index, which tracks company shares, while the consumer price index follows prices of consumer goods and services.
ww.A tax on consumers who buy goods in stor: A tax on consumers is a sales or consumption tax, and the consumer price index is a measurement tool that does not tax anyone.

rw: Fiscal policy is the use of government taxing and spending decisions to influence the economy, such as demand, jobs and growth.

ww.Company decisions on pricing and output: Company decisions on prices and output are microeconomic business choices, while fiscal policy is set by governments through taxing and spending, not by firms.
ww.Rules about trade with other nations tod: Rules about trade with other nations are trade policy, which covers tariffs and quotas, and fiscal policy concerns taxing and spending decisions at home.
ww.Central bank decisions on interest rates: Central bank decisions on interest rates are monetary policy, which is run by the central bank, and fiscal policy is run by the government.

rw: Cutting taxes and raising spending adds to total demand, which fights a recession, and that is called expansionary fiscal policy.

ww.Protectionist trade policy: Protectionist trade policy uses tariffs and quotas to shield domestic industries, and it does not involve changing government taxes and spending to boost demand.
ww.Monetary policy by banks: Monetary policy is run by the central bank through interest rates and the money supply, and tax and spending changes are made by the government.
ww.Contractionary fiscal policy: Contractionary fiscal policy raises taxes or cuts spending to cool the economy, which is the reverse of what the government is doing in a recession.

rw: Monetary policy means central bank actions, such as changing interest rates or buying bonds, to influence the money supply and credit in the economy.

ww.Government taxing and spending set by th: Government taxing and spending set by the budget is fiscal policy, and monetary policy is handled by the central bank, not by lawmakers.
ww.Business pricing strategy for goods and: Business pricing strategy is a firm-level decision about what to charge, and it is not an economy-wide tool for managing the money supply.
ww.Laws about trade between countries and f: Laws about trade between countries form trade policy, which sets tariffs and rules, and they do not control money and credit in the economy.

rw: The multiplier effect means an initial change in spending sets off rounds of income and spending, so total income changes by more than the first amount.

ww.A tax on multiple goods bought together: A tax on goods bought together has no link to the multiplier, which describes how spending spreads through the economy and not a type of tax.
ww.Prices doubling every year for all goods: Prices doubling every year describes hyperinflation, a runaway price rise, while the multiplier concerns how a change in spending grows total income.
ww.The number of firms in a market, which a: The number of firms in a market describes market structure, which affects competition, and it is not the spending effect called the multiplier.

rw: When spending exceeds tax revenue in one year, the gap is a budget deficit, which the government must cover by borrowing.

ww.A trade surplus: A trade surplus is when exports exceed imports, which relates to international trade and not to the gap between government spending and tax revenue.
ww.A budget surplus: A budget surplus is the reverse case, where tax revenue exceeds spending in a year, so it does not describe spending above revenue.
ww.The national debt: The national debt is the total accumulated borrowing over many years, while the yearly gap between spending and revenue is the deficit.

rw: Comparative advantage means a producer gives up less of other goods to make a product, which is a lower opportunity cost, and it drives gains from trade.

ww.The ability to charge more than all of t: Charging more than all other firms shows pricing power, not comparative advantage, which is about opportunity cost in producing goods and not about price levels.
ww.The ability to ban imports from all of t: Banning imports is a protectionist policy tool and not an ability to produce, so it has nothing to do with comparative advantage in trade.
ww.The ability to make more of everything t: Making more of everything than other nations is absolute advantage, and comparative advantage depends on the lowest opportunity cost, not on higher output of all goods.

rw: Country A gives up only 2 shirts per phone while B gives up 4, so A has the lower opportunity cost and the comparative advantage in phones.

ww.Country B: Country B gives up 4 shirts per phone, which is a higher opportunity cost than Country A's 2 shirts, so B does not have the advantage in phones.
ww.Both equally: The two countries have different opportunity costs, 2 shirts versus 4 shirts per phone, so they are not equal, and one must have the advantage.
ww.Neither: Opportunity costs of 2 and 4 shirts per phone differ, so one country has the lower cost, and it cannot be that neither has an advantage.

rw: A tariff is a tax placed on imported goods, which raises their price and protects domestic producers while bringing revenue to the government.

ww.A limit on exports abroad: A limit on exports is an export restriction or embargo, and a tariff is aimed at imports, not at goods leaving the country.
ww.A subsidy paid to exporters: A subsidy paid to exporters is a payment to help sellers abroad, which is the opposite of a tax collected on goods coming in.
ww.A fee charged for banks: A fee charged for banks is a financial service charge, and it has no link to the tax placed on imported goods, which is a tariff.

rw: A quota is a limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported, which restricts supply and tends to raise domestic prices.

ww.A payment to producers from the state to: A payment from the state to producers is a subsidy, which supports firms with money, while a quota limits the quantity of goods coming in.
ww.A trade agreement between two or more pa: A trade agreement between countries is a treaty that lowers barriers, and it is the opposite kind of tool from a quota, which restricts trade.
ww.A tax on imports charged by the customs: A tax on imports collected at ports is a tariff, which works through price, while a quota works by capping the quantity allowed in.

rw: A tariff makes imported steel costlier, which lets domestic steel producers raise their prices too, so domestic buyers of steel pay more.

ww.Lower taxes on steel for all domestic bu: A tariff raises the cost of imported steel, so it does not lower taxes, and it increases what buyers pay and the revenue the government collects.
ww.Lower steel prices at home for most buye: Tariffs make imports more costly, which pushes steel prices up at home, so domestic buyers pay more and not less for steel.
ww.End all steel trade for good in the nati: A tariff makes imported steel more expensive but does not stop trade completely, and some steel is still imported at the higher price.

rw: A trade deficit occurs when a country's imports are greater than its exports over a period, so it buys more from abroad than it sells.

ww.A shortage of workers: A shortage of workers is a labor market condition, and a trade deficit refers to the balance of exports and imports between nations.
ww.Exports exceed imports: Exports exceeding imports is a trade surplus, and it is the opposite of a trade deficit, where a country buys more from abroad than it sells.
ww.A fall in taxes owed: A fall in taxes owed is a tax cut, which concerns government finance and not the balance between imports and exports in trade.

rw: A stronger dollar buys more euros, so U.S. goods cost more in euro terms, which makes U.S. exports more expensive for Europeans.

ww.They are not affected by the change in v: Exchange rates affect prices abroad, so a stronger dollar does change export competitiveness, and it is wrong to say exports are not affected at all.
ww.They are banned from sale in Europe: An exchange rate change alters prices but does not legally ban any sales, so U.S. goods are still sold in Europe, only at higher euro prices.
ww.They become cheaper for Europeans to buy: A stronger dollar makes U.S. goods cost more in euros, so it is a weaker dollar, not a stronger one, that makes them cheaper for Europeans.

rw: In a command economy the government makes most decisions about what to produce, how, and at what prices, with central planning replacing market forces.

ww.Tradition decides all outcomes, so peopl: Tradition deciding all outcomes describes a traditional economy, where custom and inherited roles guide production, and not a command economy run by the government.
ww.Markets decide all outcomes through pric: Markets deciding outcomes through prices and trade describes a market economy, whereas a command economy has the state direct production and set prices.
ww.Consumers set all prices alone by their: Consumers setting all prices alone would be an extreme market view, while a command economy puts price and production choices in the hands of government.

rw: A mixed economy blends private businesses and markets with government roles like public schools and regulation, which is the description of the United States.

ww.A command economy: In a command economy the government makes most decisions, but the United States has many private firms that set their own prices, so it does not fit.
ww.A tradition economy: A tradition economy relies on custom for choices, but the United States uses markets and laws, so public schools and private firms do not match this.
ww.A barter economy: A barter economy trades goods directly without money, but the United States uses money, so private firms and public schools do not suggest barter.

rw: Pollution imposes a cost on fishers who are not part of the factory's transaction, which is a negative externality, since the factory does not pay for it.

ww.A positive externality: A positive externality is a benefit to bystanders, such as a neighbor's garden, but pollution harming fishers is a cost placed on others, so it is not positive.
ww.A public good only: A public good is something nonexcludable and nonrival like national defense, and pollution harming fishers is a spillover cost and not a public good.
ww.A subsidy for firms: A subsidy is a payment from the government to support firms, and the factory's pollution is a cost to others and not a government payment.

rw: Because people can use public goods without paying, firms cannot charge for them, which is the free-rider problem, and so private markets supply too little.

ww.They cost nothing to make for any firm i: Public goods are costly to produce, and being free of cost to make is not the reason markets underprovide them, so this is false.
ww.Everyone refuses to use them, so the gov: People generally want and use public goods, such as clean air, so the issue is not refusal to use them, but that nobody wants to pay.
ww.Prices are set too high for most of the: Public goods are not underprovided because prices are too high, and the problem is that firms cannot collect payment from free riders at any price.

rw: The business cycle is the recurring pattern of expansion and contraction in economic activity over time, seen in changes in output, jobs and incomes.

ww.A tax calendar for businesses that lists: A tax calendar lists due dates for filing and paying taxes, and it is an administrative schedule, not the pattern of economic ups and downs.
ww.A bicycle route used by delivery firms t: A bicycle route for delivery firms is a transport matter, and the word cycle here is a pun, since the business cycle concerns economic activity.
ww.A list of company products offered for s: A list of products for sale is a catalog, which has nothing to do with the pattern of growth and decline in the economy as a whole.

rw: After the peak, economic activity starts to decline, and this falling phase is called contraction, which can lead to a recession.

ww.Expansion phase: Expansion comes before the peak, when output rises, and after a peak the economy moves downward, so expansion does not follow the peak.
ww.Recovery: Recovery follows the trough, as output starts to grow again, so it comes after the bottom of the cycle and not right after a peak.
ww.The trough: The trough is the lowest point of the cycle and comes at the end of contraction, not directly after the peak, where decline only begins.

rw: Borrowers with fixed-rate loans repay with dollars that have lost purchasing power, and their incomes tend to rise with prices, so they gain.

ww.People on fixed incomes only: People on fixed incomes lose from unexpected inflation, since their income does not rise while prices do, so they cannot be the group that gains.
ww.Lenders with fixed-rate loans: Lenders with fixed-rate loans lose, because the dollars repaid are worth less in purchasing power than the dollars lent, so they are on the losing side.
ww.Savers who hold their money in cash: Savers holding cash lose purchasing power as prices rise, since their money buys less, so they are hurt by unexpected inflation and do not gain.

rw: The labor force is made up of people who are employed plus those who are unemployed and actively looking for work.

ww.All people living in a country or its re: All people living in a country is the total population, which includes children, retirees and others outside the labor force, so it is too broad.
ww.Only government workers and public emplo: Government workers are only one group of the employed, and the labor force includes private sector workers and job seekers too, so this is too narrow.
ww.Only people with full-time jobs, not par: Part-time workers are employed and count in the labor force, so limiting it to full-time jobs would leave out many people who work.

rw: Productivity is output per unit of labor, and 15 units per hour is 50 percent more than 10, so labor productivity increased.

ww.Unemployment rose slightly: Output per hour rose from 10 to 15 units, which says nothing about joblessness, so unemployment is not what the example describes.
ww.Productivity fell sharply: Output per worker rose from 10 to 15 units per hour, so productivity increased, and it did not fall at all, let alone sharply.
ww.Inflation occurred in prices: Inflation is a rise in the general price level, and the example only gives output per hour, with no price information, so it cannot show inflation.

rw: In a recession incomes and spending drop, so income and sales taxes bring in less money, and tax revenue falls.

ww.It is unaffected by the downturn at all: Tax revenue depends on income and spending, which both fall in a recession, so it is clearly affected by the downturn and is not unaffected.
ww.It becomes unlimited as incomes rise a l: Revenue cannot become unlimited, and in a recession incomes fall rather than rise, so the tax base shrinks and collections go down.
ww.It rises sharply as incomes grow in a do: Incomes do not grow in a downturn but fall, as jobs and profits drop, so tax collections shrink instead of rising sharply.

rw: Consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus price paid, so $50 minus $35 equals $15 of surplus for the buyer.

ww.$50: The $50 is the most the buyer would pay, which is the willingness to pay, and consumer surplus is that amount minus the price paid.
ww.$85: The $85 adds the willingness to pay and the price together, but surplus is found by subtracting, which gives $50 minus $35, or $15.
ww.$35: The $35 is the price actually paid, and consumer surplus is the gap between willingness to pay and price, so it is $50 minus $35, or $15.

rw: Marginal utility is the additional satisfaction a consumer gets from consuming one more unit of a good, and it usually falls as consumption grows.

ww.The price of the unit sold to the buyer: The price of a unit is what the buyer pays in the shop, which is different from marginal utility, the added satisfaction from one more unit.
ww.The cost to produce the unit for the fir: The cost to produce a unit is a firm's cost, such as marginal cost, while marginal utility is measured by the satisfaction of the consumer.
ww.The total satisfaction from all units co: Total satisfaction from all units is total utility, while marginal utility looks only at the change from the last unit consumed.

rw: Each extra slice gives less satisfaction than the one before, with the fifth slice much less enjoyable than the first, which is diminishing marginal utility.

ww.Increasing returns to scale: Increasing returns to scale describe a firm's output rising faster than inputs, which is a production idea and not about a consumer's falling enjoyment of pizza.
ww.Rising inflation for all goods: Rising inflation is a general price increase, and the pizza example is about falling satisfaction from each extra slice, not about prices changing.
ww.Perfect competition in markets: Perfect competition is a market structure of many sellers, and the pizza example describes a consumer's satisfaction falling, so it does not apply.

rw: Monopsony means a single buyer facing many sellers, as when one large employer is the only buyer of labor in a town.

ww.A market with many buyers and many selle: Many buyers and many sellers describes a competitive market, and a monopsony has only one buyer, so this is the reverse situation.
ww.A market with two sellers and many buyer: Two sellers and many buyers is a duopoly, which is a market with few sellers, and a monopsony is defined by the number of buyers.
ww.A market with only one seller and many b: One seller and many buyers is a monopoly, where the seller has the power, while a monopsony has one buyer, so these are mirror images.

rw: Quantity fell 10% and price rose 20%, so elasticity is 10 divided by 20, which equals 0.5, and a value below 1 means demand is inelastic.

ww.2.0, which is elastic: Elasticity here is percent change in quantity (10 of 100, or 10%) divided by percent change in price (2 of 10, or 20%), which is 0.5, not 2.0.
ww.1.0, which is unit elastic: Unit elasticity would need equal percent changes, but quantity fell 10% while price rose 20%, so the ratio is 0.5 and not 1.0.
ww.0.2, so perfectly inelastic: Dividing 10% by 20% gives 0.5 and not 0.2, and perfectly inelastic demand means a value of zero, not a value like 0.2.

rw: Quantity fell from 200 to 100, which is 50%, while price rose from $4 to $5, which is 25%, so elasticity is 50 divided by 25, or 2, and elastic.

ww.Perfectly inelastic, because quantity fe: Quantity fell 50 percent, which is a large drop, so demand is not perfectly inelastic, a case where quantity would not respond to price at all.
ww.Unit elastic, because quantity and price: Unit elastic demand needs equal percent changes, but quantity fell 50% while price rose only 25%, so the responses are not the same.
ww.Inelastic, because revenue rose after th: Revenue went from $4 times 200, or $800, down to $5 times 100, or $500, so revenue fell, and falling revenue after a price rise means elastic demand.

rw: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percent than the price rises, so the gain per unit is larger than the loss in sales, and revenue rises.

ww.Revenue becomes zero: Revenue does not drop to zero, since buyers with inelastic demand keep buying nearly the same amount even at a higher price, so sales remain.
ww.Total revenue falls: Revenue falls with a price rise only when demand is elastic, but inelastic demand means quantity drops by a smaller percent than price rises.
ww.Revenue stays the same: Revenue would stay the same only with unit elastic demand, but with inelastic demand the price increase outweighs the small drop in quantity.

rw: With elastic demand, a price cut raises quantity sold by a larger percent than the price fell, so price times quantity grows and revenue rises.

ww.Revenue doubles surely: Revenue cannot be guaranteed to double, and a $5 price cut on a $50 ticket is only 10%, so any gain is limited by the quantity response.
ww.Total revenue falls: Revenue falls after a price cut when demand is inelastic, but this demand is elastic, so the increase in tickets sold outweighs the lower price.
ww.Revenue stays the same: Revenue stays the same only if demand is unit elastic, but elastic demand responds more than proportionally, so the price cut changes revenue upward.

rw: A normal good is one for which demand rises as consumer income rises, such as restaurant meals, so people buy more when they earn more.

ww.A good whose demand falls as the income: Demand that falls as income rises describes an inferior good, such as store-brand noodles, and it is the opposite of a normal good.
ww.A good that everyone buys each year at t: Buying the same amount each year regardless of income is not a normal good, which is defined by how demand responds to income changes.
ww.A good with no substitutes in the market: Having no substitutes is a matter of elasticity, and normal good status concerns demand and income, not whether alternatives exist.

rw: Demand that falls as income rises defines an inferior good, and shoppers move from store-brand noodles to restaurant meals when they earn more.

ww.A normal good: A normal good has rising demand when income rises, and since demand for store-brand noodles falls as incomes rise, they are not a normal good.
ww.A complement: Complements are goods used together, like noodles and sauce, and the example links demand to income and not to another good's price.
ww.A public good: A public good is nonrival and nonexcludable, like street lighting, and the example describes demand falling as income rises, which is not a public good.

rw: Ceteris paribus is Latin for other things equal, meaning economists hold all other factors constant to study how one variable changes an outcome.

ww.Everything changes at once for all: If everything changed at once, effects could not be separated, but ceteris paribus does the opposite by isolating one cause at a time.
ww.Supply always equals demand in markets: Supply and demand do not always match, and the phrase is a method for analysis and not a claim about market equilibrium.
ww.All prices rise together each year: The phrase says nothing about prices rising together, and it means holding other factors constant to see the effect of changing one thing.

rw: A change in a good's own price changes quantity demanded, which is shown as movement along the existing demand curve and not as a shift of it.

ww.A change in elasticity only now: A change in price moves quantity demanded along the curve, and elasticity measures the size of that response, so it is not a separate change.
ww.A shift of the demand curve right: A rightward shift of the demand curve comes from non-price factors such as income or tastes, and a price change alone only moves along the curve.
ww.A shift of the supply curve right: A rightward shift of the supply curve means more is supplied at every price, and the example describes buyers responding to a price rise, which is demand.

rw: A health study raises consumers' taste for blueberries, so they want more at every price, which shifts the demand curve to the right.

ww.It shifts left: A shift left would show a fall in demand, but good news about blueberries raises buyers' interest at every price, so the curve shifts right.
ww.It becomes vertical: A vertical demand curve means perfectly inelastic demand, which is a statement about price response, and news about health benefits does not make the curve vertical.
ww.It does not move: The study changes consumer tastes and preferences, which are non-price determinants of demand, so the curve does move and cannot stay in place.

rw: A technology that lowers production costs makes sellers willing to supply more at every price, which shifts the supply curve to the right.

ww.An increase in input prices for all firm: Higher input prices raise production costs, so firms supply less at each price and the supply curve shifts left, not right.
ww.Fewer sellers entering the market in the: Fewer sellers means less is supplied at each price, so the supply curve shifts left, and it cannot shift right.
ww.A tax on producers who make the goods in: A tax on producers raises their costs and reduces the amount they supply at each price, so the supply curve shifts left.

rw: The frost cuts the crop and so the orange juice supply, which shifts the supply curve left and raises the equilibrium price.

ww.Neither curve moves in the market: A frost damages the orange crop, so the supply of oranges changes, and at least one curve must move in the market for orange juice.
ww.Demand shifts left and the price rises: The frost affects producers and not buyers' tastes or incomes, so demand does not shift, and the supply curve is what moves in this case.
ww.Supply shifts right and the price falls: A frost reduces the oranges available, so supply decreases and shifts left, not right, and a leftward shift raises the price instead of lowering it.

rw: Rising demand pushes price up and falling supply pushes price up, so both shifts raise the price, while the effect on quantity is unclear.

ww.It falls: A fall in price would need demand to decrease or supply to increase, but here demand rises and supply falls, and both push the price up.
ww.Unclear: Quantity is unclear because the shifts push in opposite directions, but price is clear, since both shifts raise it, so the price effect is known.
ww.No change: No change in price would need the two shifts to offset, but increased demand and decreased supply both raise price, so it must rise.

rw: Supply of 180 exceeds demand of 120 by 60 units, which is a surplus, and sellers will cut prices to clear the market, so price tends to fall.

ww.A shortage of 60, so price tends to rise: Quantity supplied of 180 exceeds quantity demanded of 120, which is a surplus and not a shortage, so price tends to fall and not rise.
ww.A surplus of 300 units, so price will fa: The gap is 180 minus 120, which is 60 units, not 300, since 300 adds the two quantities together instead of finding the difference.
ww.Equilibrium at $8 with no gap at all: Equilibrium needs quantity demanded to equal quantity supplied, but 120 and 180 differ, so $8 is not the equilibrium price and a gap exists.

rw: Setting 100 minus 2P equal to 20 plus 2P gives 80 equals 4P, so P equals $20, where both quantities equal 60.

ww.$30: At $30, Qd is 100 minus 60, or 40, and Qs is 20 plus 60, or 80, so supply exceeds demand and $30 is not the equilibrium price.
ww.$10: At $10, Qd is 100 minus 20, or 80, and Qs is 20 plus 20, or 40, so demand exceeds supply and $10 is too low.
ww.$40: At $40, Qd is 100 minus 80, or 20, while Qs is 20 plus 80, or 100, which is a large surplus, so $40 is not equilibrium.

rw: The equilibrium price is $20, so Qd equals 100 minus 2 times 20, which is 60, and Qs equals 20 plus 40, which is also 60.

ww.80 units: The 80 units is the quantity demanded at $10, but at the equilibrium price of $20, 100 minus 40 gives 60 units, so 80 is wrong.
ww.120 units: The 120 is more than the quantity demanded even at a price of zero, which is 100, so it cannot be the equilibrium quantity.
ww.20 units: The 20 is the intercept of the supply curve at a price of zero, and at the equilibrium price of $20 quantity is 60, not 20.

rw: A change in demand is a shift of the whole curve from non-price factors, and a change in quantity demanded is movement along the curve caused by price.

ww.Quantity demanded changes without a pric: Quantity demanded changes with the good's own price, while income, tastes or related prices shift the entire demand curve, so this reverses the two ideas.
ww.They are the same thing and mean exactly: The terms mean different things in economics, since one is a shift of the curve and the other a movement along it, so they cannot be swapped.
ww.A change in demand is caused only by a c: Price changes move quantity demanded along the curve, while income, tastes and related goods shift demand itself, so demand is not caused only by price.

rw: Utility is the satisfaction or benefit a person gets from consuming a good or service, and consumers weigh it against price when they choose.

ww.The cost of electricity used by a househ: The cost of electricity is a household bill, and in economics the word utility means satisfaction, not the power company service you pay for.
ww.A tax paid by firms and people on the go: A tax paid on goods is a sales or excise tax, and utility in economics refers to the satisfaction gained from using something, not a tax.
ww.A trade barrier set by a government to l: A trade barrier such as a tariff or quota is a trade policy, and it has nothing to do with the satisfaction consumers gain from goods.

rw: Marginal utility of the third slice is the extra satisfaction it adds, which is 8 utils, and it is lower than the second slice, showing diminishing returns.

ww.20 utils: The 20 utils is the marginal utility of the first slice, not the third, because marginal utility is the extra satisfaction of the specific slice.
ww.14 utils: The 14 utils is the extra satisfaction from the second slice, and the third slice adds only 8 utils, so 14 is the wrong slice.
ww.42 utils: The 42 utils is the total utility of all three slices (20 plus 14 plus 8), and marginal utility is only the extra from the last slice.

rw: Most resources are scarce and using them means giving up other uses, so goods have an opportunity cost, and truly free goods are rare.

ww.Because they cannot be consumed by anyon: A free good can be consumed, and economists call goods free because they are so plentiful they carry no opportunity cost, so this reason is false.
ww.Because governments ban them from sale i: Governments do not ban free goods, and they are rare simply because most resources are limited, so this gives an invented reason.
ww.Because prices are always zero for every: Prices are not zero for every good, since most goods cost something, and that fact is the reason free goods are rare, not a cause of it.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, and studying the extra 2 hours costs her the $30 babysitting job.

ww.The first 2 hours spent: The first 2 hours would be spent anyway to earn a B, and the extra time is what costs her, so those hours are not the opportunity cost here.
ww.No cost to speak of: Giving up a $30 babysitting job is a real cost, so saying there is no cost ignores the next best alternative she sacrificed.
ww.The A grade she earns: The A grade is the benefit she gains by studying longer, while opportunity cost is the value of what she gives up, which is the job.

rw: A market brings buyers and sellers together so they can trade goods and services, whether in a physical place, online, or elsewhere.

ww.To ban trade between buyers and sellers: Markets exist to allow trade, so banning trade between buyers and sellers is the opposite of the purpose of a market.
ww.To produce goods only, and never to sell: Markets are where goods are exchanged, so producing goods only and never selling them contradicts the purpose of a market, which is exchange.
ww.To fix prices by law for all goods and s: Markets let prices adjust through buyers and sellers interacting, and fixing prices by law is a feature of controlled economies, not the purpose of a market.

rw: Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers of identical products, so each is a price taker who cannot influence the market price.

ww.Differentiated brands that each have the: Differentiated brands with loyal buyers describe monopolistic competition, where firms have some pricing power, while perfect competition has identical products.
ww.One seller with no rivals at all in the: One seller with no rivals describes a monopoly, which is the opposite end of the spectrum from perfect competition, with its many sellers.
ww.A few large firms that dominate the whol: A few large firms dominating the market describes an oligopoly, and perfect competition has many small firms with none holding much power.

rw: A farmer who cannot influence the price sells identical wheat among many sellers, which are the traits of perfect competition and price takers.

ww.A monopoly firm: A monopoly firm is the only seller and sets its own price, but a wheat farmer has no such power and takes the market price.
ww.An oligopoly firm: An oligopoly has a few large firms that can influence prices, while a wheat farmer is one of thousands and cannot affect the market price.
ww.Monopolistic rivalry: Monopolistic competition has differentiated products and some pricing power, while wheat is identical, so one farmer cannot influence the market price.

rw: Monopolistic competition has many sellers with differentiated products, such as different brands, while perfect competition has identical products, which is the key difference.

ww.Firms are price fixers by law, as the go: Firms in monopolistic competition set their own prices in the market and not by law, so government price fixing is not the key difference.
ww.There are no sellers at all in any singl: Both market structures have many sellers, so saying there are no sellers is false, and sellers exist in every market structure.
ww.There is only one seller in the whole ma: One seller in the whole market describes a monopoly, and monopolistic competition has many sellers, so the number of sellers is not one.

rw: Restaurants in a city are many sellers offering differentiated products, like menus and atmosphere, with easy entry, which matches monopolistic competition.

ww.Two major aircraft makers: Two major aircraft makers form a duopoly, a type of oligopoly with very few sellers, and not a market with many differentiated sellers.
ww.A wheat farm nearby: A wheat farm sells an identical product alongside many other farms, which matches perfect competition and not differentiated products.
ww.The local water utility: A local water utility is usually a natural monopoly with one seller and no rivals, which is unlike a market with many differentiated sellers.

rw: Game theory analyzes strategic decisions where each party's outcome depends on the choices of others, as with firms setting prices in an oligopoly.

ww.Measuring GDP and the total output of wh: Measuring GDP and national output is the work of macroeconomic accounting, and game theory is a tool for studying strategic choices instead.
ww.Designing video games and the rules that: Game theory in economics is a mathematical way to study strategy and has nothing to do with designing video games for screens.
ww.Setting wages for workers in firms acros: Setting wages across industries is a labor market question, and game theory instead studies how interdependent decisions interact in strategic settings.

rw: Cutting fares is the best move whatever the rival does, yet both cutting leaves both worse off, which is the structure of the prisoner's dilemma.

ww.Perfect competition: Perfect competition has many small firms that are price takers, while two airlines watching each other's fares are in a strategic situation, which fits game theory.
ww.Comparative advantage: Comparative advantage is about lower opportunity costs in trade, and the fare scenario is about rivals' strategic choices leading to a worse joint result.
ww.A command economy here: A command economy is a system where government plans production, and the two airlines are private firms in a strategic choice, not a planned economy.

rw: A price taker is a firm that must accept the price set by the market, because it is too small to change it and sells identical goods.

ww.A firm that sets prices, with no close r: A firm that sets prices with no close rivals is a price maker, such as a monopoly, which is the opposite of a price taker.
ww.A government agency that sets taxes: A government agency that sets taxes works in public finance and has no role in the market price, so it is not a price taker.
ww.A customer who negotiates the price: A customer who negotiates the price is bargaining, which describes a buyer's behavior, while a price taker is a seller that cannot change the price.

rw: Deadweight loss is the surplus lost when beneficial trades do not happen because of a distortion, such as a tax, ceiling or monopoly pricing.

ww.A tax refund that the government sends b: A tax refund is money returned to a person by the government, which is a transfer and not the lost surplus called deadweight loss.
ww.A profit that a firm earns when it sells: Profit from selling above cost is a gain for the firm, while deadweight loss is a loss of total surplus that nobody receives.
ww.A subsidy payment that the government gi: A subsidy payment is a transfer from government to producers, and while subsidies can create deadweight loss, the payment itself is not the loss.

rw: A binding price ceiling stops trades that would benefit both buyers and sellers, so total surplus shrinks, and that lost surplus is deadweight loss.

ww.A bigger surplus: A ceiling blocks some trades and reduces total surplus, so surplus gets smaller and does not get bigger, which is the reverse of this option.
ww.Higher profits: Sellers receive a lower price under a binding ceiling and sell fewer units, so profits tend to fall and not rise.
ww.More competition: A ceiling restricts how the market works and does not add rivals, and the blocked trades reduce the number of deals, not increase competition.

rw: Rational self-interest assumes people weigh costs and benefits and choose what maximizes their own benefit, which is the basic behavioral assumption of economics.

ww.The assumption that people always give t: Rational self-interest does not mean people always give to charity, and it assumes people act to improve their own situation, not to help others first.
ww.The assumption of random choice by buyer: Random choice would contradict rationality, since the assumption is that buyers and sellers choose deliberately to get the most benefit from their options.
ww.The assumption that people never trade,: People trade with one another in markets, and the assumption says nothing about avoiding trade, so each household making all its needs is not the idea.

rw: Asymmetric information is when one party to a deal knows more than the other, such as a seller who knows a product's hidden defects.

ww.Market equilibrium: Market equilibrium is where supply equals demand, which concerns price and quantity and not what each side of a deal knows.
ww.Public information: Public information is known to everyone, so both parties have it, and that is the opposite of one side knowing something the other lacks.
ww.Symmetric information: Symmetric information means both sides know the same facts, so it is the reverse of the situation where one side knows more.

rw: The seller knows the car is defective while the buyer does not, so information is unequal, which is asymmetric information and creates risk for buyers.

ww.Comparative advantage: Comparative advantage is about lower opportunity costs in production, and it does not explain the risk buyers face when a seller hides a defect.
ww.Economies of scale: Economies of scale describe lower average costs from larger output, and they do not address a buyer's lack of knowledge about a car's condition.
ww.Diminishing returns: Diminishing returns describe falling extra output from added inputs, and they do not relate to one side of a deal knowing hidden facts.

rw: Marginal cost is the change in total cost, so $560 minus $500 equals $60 for the 11th unit.

ww.$560: The $560 is the total cost of 11 units, and marginal cost is the change in total cost from making one more unit, which is $560 minus $500.
ww.$51: The $51 is not found by any valid step, since marginal cost is the extra total cost of the 11th unit, which is $560 minus $500, or $60.
ww.$50: The $50 is the average cost of the first 10 units ($500 divided by 10), but marginal cost is $560 minus $500, which equals $60.

rw: Revenue is 800 times $25, or $20,000, variable cost is 800 times $15, or $12,000, and subtracting fixed costs of $5,000 leaves $3,000.

ww.$20,000: The $20,000 equals 800 times $25 and is only revenue, and profit must subtract variable costs of $12,000 and fixed costs of $5,000.
ww.$8,000: The $8,000 equals revenue minus variable cost ($20,000 minus $12,000) and forgets to subtract the fixed costs of $5,000, so profit is $3,000.
ww.$12,000: The $12,000 is just the total variable cost (800 times $15), and profit is revenue of $20,000 minus $12,000 minus $5,000, which is $3,000.

rw: Contribution per unit is $30 minus $18, or $12, and break-even units equal $12,000 divided by $12, which is 1,000 units.

ww.400 units: Dividing $12,000 by 30 gives 400, but that ignores variable cost, since each unit contributes only $12, so the answer is 1,000 units.
ww.667 units: The 667 comes from dividing $12,000 by $18, the variable cost, but break-even uses the contribution of $12, which gives 1,000 units.
ww.2,000 units: The 2,000 comes from a wrong contribution of $6, and the right figure is $30 minus $18, or $12, so $12,000 divided by $12 is 1,000.

rw: Margin of safety is the gap between actual or expected sales and break-even sales, showing how far sales can fall before the firm starts losing money.

ww.The cost of safety gear for the workers: Safety gear costs for workers have no link to the idea, which is a financial measure of how much sales can drop before profits vanish.
ww.The tax rate on the firm's profits for t: A tax rate on profits is a different measure, and margin of safety compares sales to the break-even point, not to taxes owed.
ww.The number of units in stock, held in th: Units in stock describe inventory, and margin of safety measures how far sales exceed break-even, which has nothing to do with the warehouse.

rw: Margin of safety equals expected sales minus break-even sales, so 1,500 minus 1,000 is 500 units that sales can fall before losses begin.

ww.2,500 units: The 2,500 adds expected sales of 1,500 to break-even of 1,000, but margin of safety is found by subtracting, giving 500 units.
ww.150 units: The 150 has no basis in the numbers, and margin of safety in units is expected sales minus break-even sales, which is 1,500 minus 1,000.
ww.1,000 units: The 1,000 is the break-even point itself, while margin of safety is the amount by which expected sales of 1,500 exceed it.

rw: With high fixed costs, a small change in sales causes a larger change in profit, and that sensitivity is what operating leverage describes.

ww.The interest rate on the loans that the: Interest on bank loans concerns financial leverage and borrowing costs, while operating leverage depends on the fixed cost share of the cost structure.
ww.The use of borrowed money to buy assets: Using borrowed money to buy assets is financial leverage, which concerns debt, and operating leverage is about fixed versus variable costs.
ww.The inventory level held in the warehous: Inventory held at year-end is a stock measure, and it does not describe how profit responds to changes in sales through fixed costs.

rw: Firm A has high fixed costs, so each extra sale adds a large contribution once costs are covered, which makes its profit swing more with sales.

ww.Firm B: Firm B has low fixed costs and high variable costs, so its costs move with sales and its profit changes less when sales change.
ww.Neither: The two firms have different cost structures, so they differ in operating leverage, and one of them must have bigger profit swings.
ww.Both alike: The firms have opposite cost structures, so they cannot be alike, and the one with higher fixed costs has the greater swing in profit.

rw: Average variable cost is total variable cost divided by the quantity of output, which tells the variable cost per unit produced.

ww.Total cost divided by the total output: Total cost divided by output is average total cost, which includes fixed costs as well as variable costs, so it is a different measure.
ww.Revenue divided by the output sold: Revenue divided by output sold is the average price or average revenue, and it is not a cost measure at all.
ww.Fixed cost divided by the total output: Fixed cost divided by output is average fixed cost, which falls as output rises, and it covers only fixed costs and not variable ones.

rw: Total cost is $1,000 plus $1,400, or $2,400, and dividing by 200 units gives an average total cost of $12 per unit.

ww.$5: The $5 is just average fixed cost ($1,000 divided by 200), and average total cost must include variable cost as well.
ww.$2,400: The $2,400 is the total cost, and average total cost divides it by the 200 units produced, which gives $12.
ww.$7: The $7 is only the average variable cost ($1,400 divided by 200), and average total cost adds the $5 of average fixed cost to give $12.

rw: In the long run a firm can adjust all inputs, such as buildings and equipment, so no costs are fixed and all costs are variable.

ww.Rent only, since rent is fixed always: Rent is fixed only in the short run, and in the long run a firm can move or change leases, so it is not fixed.
ww.Wages only, since wages are fixed: Wages can be changed by hiring, firing or renegotiating over time, so it is wrong to say that wages are fixed in the long run.
ww.All costs, since all costs are fixed: Fixed costs belong to the short run, when some inputs cannot change, and the long run lets every input vary, so all costs are not fixed.
